title: Unions and Universities Sue Over USCIS Green Card Rules Targeting Adjustment of Status
excerpt: The federal lawsuit challenges a May policy that treats seeking a green card from inside the US as a negative factor and an August policy letting officers deny applications without requesting more evidence — even for cases filed before the rules existed.
body:
• Immigrant families, workers, university educators and unions filed suit in federal court this week challenging two USCIS policies that make it far harder for eligible immigrants already in the United States to obtain green cards without leaving the country.
  • A May 2026 policy directs officers to treat an applicant's decision to seek adjustment of status from inside the US — rather than going abroad for consular processing — as a negative discretionary factor, requiring applicants to show "unusual or even outstanding" considerations to overcome it.
  • An August 2026 policy lets officers deny applications without first issuing a request for evidence or notice of intent to deny — and applies retroactively to cases filed before the policy existed.
  • What pending applicants should do now: keep complete copies of every filing, respond immediately to any request for evidence, and consult an immigration attorney — the rules may change if the court blocks the policies, but they apply to pending cases in the meantime.

Immigrant families, workers, university educators and advocacy groups have filed a federal lawsuit challenging two new U.S. immigration policies that they say could force some eligible green card applicants to leave the country to pursue permanent residence — separating them from their families and jobs, according to the American Immigration Lawyers Association and reporting by IANS.

The lawsuit, filed this week, targets policies issued by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services in May and August that fundamentally alter adjustment of status — the process Congress created to let eligible immigrants already in the United States seek lawful permanent residence without applying for an immigrant visa at a U.S. consulate abroad.

Two policies under challenge

The first, the Adjustment of Status policy issued in May 2026, directs USCIS officers to treat an applicant's decision to seek permanent residence from inside the United States, rather than leaving the country for consular processing, as a negative factor when exercising discretion. Applicants must then demonstrate "unusual or even outstanding" considerations to overcome that negative factor — a standard the plaintiffs say flips decades of practice on its head.

The second, the Evidence, Requests for Evidence, and Notices of Intent to Deny policy issued in August 2026, allows officers to deny applications without first giving applicants an opportunity to submit additional evidence. Crucially, the challengers say that policy also applies to applications that were already pending when it was issued — moving the goalposts on people who filed under the earlier rules.

The plaintiffs are asking the court to block and ultimately set aside both policies and to require USCIS to adjudicate affected applications under what they contend is controlling legal precedent. The case, American Association of University Professors et al. v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security et al., remains pending, and the allegations have not been adjudicated.

"For decades, people who met the requirements to apply for a green card from inside the United States were able to do so without having that choice count against them."

— Leslie Dellon, Senior Attorney for Business Immigration, American Immigration Council

Who is suing

The organizational plaintiffs cut across academia, labor and immigrant advocacy: the American Association of University Professors and its Harvard and Boston University chapters, the Service Employees International Union and its Local 509 and 32BJ chapters, and Americans for Immigrant Justice. Six individual green card applicants are also named. They are represented by Democracy Forward, the American Immigration Council, the American Immigration Lawyers Association and the firm Colombo & Hurd.

"Our immigration system should embody the values that define America: fairness, transparency, due process, and adherence to the rule of law," said AILA President Jeff Joseph. "No administration should be permitted to rewrite the rules unilaterally or place itself above the law."

AAUP President Todd Wolfson framed the suit as a defense of American research itself: "By weaponizing the green card process and threatening immigrant professors, researchers, and students with sudden deportation or forced family separation, this administration is sabotaging scientific innovation and turning our universities into hostile environments for the global talent that drives our country forward."

Diaspora angle: the backlog generation pays first

Indian nationals are the largest cohort in the employment-based green card queue, facing waits that stretch years — even decades — under per-country caps. That makes them the likeliest casualties of a policy that penalizes staying in the country while your application is processed. An applicant who has built a career, paid taxes and waited their turn for years could now be told that choosing to adjust status from home is a strike against them — or have a pending case denied without a chance to supply missing evidence.

"This is a major shift with very real consequences: spouses and parents separated from their families, workers forced to leave their jobs, students and researchers yanked away from their work, and people potentially stranded abroad for months or even years waiting for a consular appointment," Dellon said.

What's next

The case will now move through the federal courts, where the plaintiffs will seek preliminary relief blocking the policies while the challenge proceeds. Separately, the administration's green card agenda faces pressure on another front: Maryland and 21 other states plus Washington, D.C., and New York City are suing over the revamped public-charge rule that penalizes green card applicants for using government benefits. For the hundreds of thousands of applicants in the queue, the legal calendar — not the agency's — now decides the rules of the game.
